A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PolyJuice and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched reliably despite relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-success, detector-calibration, resolution-transfer, image-quality, and prompt-generalization experiments in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds distribution-level image-quality results and transferred DiffPGD attack comparisons.

M1.justification: The SPCA/HSIC direction computation, latent-steering procedure, and resolution interpolation remain unchanged in Sections 2–3 and Algorithm 1. The new threat-model summary restates the existing procedure; Appendix D proposes possible defenses without incorporating them into PolyJuice.

E1.justification: Both versions use COCO and PartiPrompts for the same image-generation, detector-attack, and calibration tasks. The new experiments retain existing data coverage and generator/detector configurations; the larger quality-evaluation sample does not introduce a new population or task.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates PolyJuice principally against unsteered generation and discusses DiffPGD only as prior work. v2 Appendix C.6 and Table 11 add regular and realistic transferred DiffPGD variants, using a ResNet-50 surrogate of RINE with FLUX[dev] and SDv3.5. This introduces the first evaluated competing attack method.

E3.justification: v2 adds two substantive evaluation protocols: distributional quality assessment using 50K real COCO images and 50K images per FLUX[sch] condition at 256×256, and surrogate-based DiffPGD transfer testing. The former introduces FID, CleanFID, precision, recall, density, and coverage. Existing direction-finding, calibration, and 1,000-image attack-evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5 extends the existing image-quality analysis with distribution-level fidelity and diversity checks in Table 5. The CLIP quality/alignment analysis already appeared in v1 Appendix C.5; hyperparameter sensitivity, spectral fingerprints, prompt-category analyses, and qualitative failure cases are retained. Appendix D contains proposed defenses, not defense experiments.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 0 for attack generation and retain Table 1's mean and standard deviation across configurations. v2 introduces no repeated-run analysis, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantive comparative findings. Table 11 reports regular/realistic transferred DiffPGD success rates of 57.2/70.1% for FLUX[dev] and 23.5/32.1% for SDv3.5, versus PolyJuice's 81.2% and 99.7%. Table 5 adds distributional results, including unsteered versus PolyJuice FID of 17.65 versus 17.23 and density of 0.585 versus 0.764. Existing matched results, including the relocated CLIP scores, are unchanged.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, equations 1–7, eigenspace derivation, and mathematical content of the algorithms are unchanged. The explicit threat model restates existing access assumptions, and the proposed defense discussion supplies no new formal result or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims of black-box universal red teaming, efficient reusable steering, cross-resolution transfer, and improved detector calibration. The new experiments support these claims without redefining the principal contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds an interpretation of increased density and asserts that the quality metrics rule out degradation-based evasion, strengthening v1's more cautious interpretation. Appendix D newly proposes collapsing TP/FN clusters through invariant or fair representation learning. This defense is untested, and its description of steering as orthogonal to the shift conflicts with Section 3.1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-webpage pointer and documents the ResNet-50 surrogate and response-matching setup for the new comparison. Existing generator identifiers, sampling parameters, LOBPCG implementation, Optuna search, and eight-A6000 hardware description remain unchanged. Detailed surrogate-training and attack budgets are not provided.

R1.justification: v2 adds nine references supporting distributional quality metrics and connections to fairness and invariant representation learning, including U-FaTE. The existing related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain essentially unchanged; DiffPGD was already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The image-quality discussion moves from Appendix C.5 into an expanded main-text Section 5. v2 also adds a structured threat-model summary, transferred-attack and defense subsections, acknowledgements, and a revised internship footnote. Most inherited prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5 and 11 and reformats v1 Table 8 as main-text Table 6. Figure 8 redisplays v1 Figure 15's gallery, which is also retained as v2 Figure 16. Other changes involve local figure/table placement, colored links, and pagination rather than a wholesale visual redesign.

improvement.justification: The transferred-attack comparison and distribution-level quality tests provide useful evidence beyond v1's unsteered baselines and CLIP metrics, while the threat-model summary improves clarity. The gain is limited by missing surrogate-training and attack-budget details, the overly strong claim that aggregate metrics rule out degradation, and Appendix D's inconsistent orthogonality explanation. These weaknesses temper the added empirical support without outweighing it.
